summary: Verified by abstract or document text: Taiwanese dynamometer tests (Tsai et al. 2003-2026) show scooter exhaust is mostly light alkanes (isopentane, methylpentanes), toluene and other aromatics, olefins, with formaldehyde and acetaldehyde as main aldehydes. Emissions rise with age, mileage and poor maintenance (about 1.9 times VOC per litre at high mileage; a three-bike Taichung case study found 14 times CO and 32 times HC for deteriorated Phase IV vs Phase VII), and cold starts raise CO and HC. Odour thresholds differ by orders of magnitude (Nagata: acetaldehyde 0.0015 ppm, acrolein 0.0036, toluene 0.33, benzene 2.7), and the dominant alkanes smell only at several ppm; CO is odourless (WHO), so smell marks the plume, not its toxic content. IARC lists benzene and formaldehyde as Group 1 hazards and gasoline exhaust as 2B; WHO recommends no safe benzene level. No measurement of pedestrians at a red light, no odour-symptom study and no confirmed resident survey was found.

findings.claim: Dynamometer tests of Taiwanese Phase III 2- and 4-stroke motorcycles: dominant VOCs isopentane, 2-methylpentane, 3-methylpentane, toluene; dominant carbonyls formaldehyde, acetaldehyde, acetone. In-use 2-stroke bikes emitted about 4.8 times the total VOC of new 2-stroke bikes (1479 vs 311 mg/km); for 4-stroke the in-use/new difference was only about 1.3 times (433 vs 344).
findings.value: Isopentane 53 (2-stroke)/295 (4-stroke) mg/km; 2-methylpentane 75/83; 3-methylpentane 34/66; toluene 30/100; total VOC 311/344 (new 2-/4-stroke), 1479/433 (in-use); formaldehyde 0.4 (new)/0.7 (in-use) mg/km; acetaldehyde 0.6/1.2; acetone 0.5/0.7; total carbonyls 3.2/3.1 (new), 5.3/4.6 (in-use)
findings.citation: Tsai J.-H., Liu Y.-Y., Yang C.-Y., Chiang H.-L., Chang L.-P. (2003) Volatile organic profiles and photochemical potentials from motorcycle engine exhaust. J. Air & Waste Manag. Assoc. 53(5):516-522
findings.quote: The dominant volatile organic carbon (VOC) species were isopentane (53 and 295 mg/km, 2- and 4-stroke, respectively), 2-methylpentane (75 and 83 mg/km), 3-methylpentane (34 and 66 mg/km), and toluene (30 and 100 mg/km).
findings.caveats: Per-km over the ECE cycle (idle, acceleration, 30 and 50 km/h cruise, deceleration); no idle-only figures in the abstract. Phase III (old) bikes, 10 new + 15 in-use. Benzene and 1,3-butadiene not among the listed dominant species. Carbonyl factors are in mg/km, tiny beside the alkane/toluene VOCs.
findings.verifierNote: Numbers all match the PubMed abstract (read by me). Original 'several times more' applied to both engine types; it holds only for 2-stroke. Crossref confirms authors, journal, volume, pages, DOI.
findings.useOnSite: Taiwanese dynamometer tests of Phase III scooters/motorcycles found exhaust dominated by light alkanes and toluene, with formaldehyde and acetaldehyde the main aldehydes; 2-stroke in-use bikes emitted several times more VOC than new ones.

findings.claim: Taiwanese four-stroke motorcycles: VOC per litre of fuel rose from 25.2 to 47.1 g/L between low-mileage and high-mileage bikes (about 1.9 times); main VOCs toluene, isopentane, xylenes, ethylbenzene, benzene.
findings.value: VOC 25.2 +/- 8.0 g/L at 5,231 +/- 4,353 km vs 47.1 +/- 19.8 g/L at 47,617 +/- 8,568 km; paraffins 38-45%, olefins 9.7-15%, aromatics 38-48%, carbonyls 1.8-3.0%; Phase III vs Phase V: CO +156%, HC +84% (Phase IV: +48%, +9%)
findings.citation: Tsai J.-H., Yao Y.-C., Huang P.-H., Chiang H.-L. (2018) Fuel economy and volatile organic compound exhaust emission for motorcycles with various running mileages. Aerosol Air Qual. Res. 18(12):3056-3067
findings.quote: Based on fuel economy, the emission factors of a total of 67 volatile organic compounds(VOCs) were 25.2 ± 8.0 g L–1 for a running mileage of 5,231 ± 4,353 km, with emissions increasing to 47.1 ± 19.8 g L–1 for a running mileage of 47,617 ± 8,568 km.
findings.caveats: Abstract only (OpenAlex). Mileage and regulation phase are confounded. Four-stroke only. No stated sample size per mileage group in the abstract.
findings.verifierNote: Numbers verified in abstract. The 156%/84% figures are Phase III relative to Phase V.
findings.useOnSite: Higher-mileage four-stroke bikes emitted about twice the VOC per litre of fuel in Taiwanese testing.

findings.claim: Newer-standard Taiwanese four-stroke motorcycles emit less BTEX and CO/HC than older ones; OFP was high in older high-mileage bikes.
findings.value: BTEX down 37-58% (Phase IV) and 44-62% (Phase V) vs Phase III; CO ratio IV/III 0.66, V/III 0.42; HC 0.61, 0.57; Phase V total VOC 0.59 g/km (lowest); 40 bikes, 52 VOCs; NOx rose with newer phases
findings.citation: Tsai J.-H., Yao Y.-C., Huang P.-H., Chiang H.-L. (2017) Criteria pollutants and volatile organic compounds emitted from motorcycle exhaust under various regulation phases. Aerosol Air Qual. Res. 17(5):1214-1223
findings.quote: Exhaust from motorcycles deteriorates with age and mileage.
findings.caveats: Abstract only. Cycle-average, not idle-specific. Ages and phases confounded.
findings.verifierNote: Verified in abstract via OpenAlex; Crossref metadata matches.
findings.useOnSite: Taiwanese tests show exhaust worsens with age and mileage and tighter standards cut BTEX.

findings.claim: Taichung case study of three targeted motorcycles: emissions were predominantly governed by engine technology and maintenance status rather than driving pattern. Deteriorated Phase IV high-emitters were fuel-rich and emitted far more CO, HC and VOC than Phase VII.
findings.value: Phase IV/VII ratio 14.0 (CO), 32.1 (HC); CO 6.36-6.94% and fuel use up to 0.138 L/km in IV-H; total VOC 22-28 times; paraffins 30.5-52.2%, aromatics 29.3-44.4%; OFP 22-52 times; lower idling share in the 2025 driving cycle than 2014
findings.citation: Tsai J.-H., How V., He Z.-J., Chan Y.-C., Chiang H.-L. (2026) Characteristics of driving pattern and motorcycle emissions during the transition of urban transportation system: A case study of Taichung in Taiwan. Results in Engineering 32:112353
findings.quote: vehicle emission characteristics were predominantly governed by engine technology and maintenance status rather than driving pattern variations
findings.caveats: Only three vehicles; ratios are case-study values, not fleet averages. Abstract only. Crossref lists issue date as December 2026 (volume 32), so cite as 2026 and check the final date before print. Does not show idle itself is the cause.
findings.verifierNote: All numbers verified in abstract (OpenAlex). Original said 'regardless of driving pattern'; the source says 'predominantly governed by ... rather than'. Reworded.
findings.useOnSite: A small Taichung case study found badly maintained old (Phase IV) motorcycles emitted tens of times more hydrocarbons than a new (Phase VII) one.

findings.claim: Cold-start motorcycle driving gave higher CO and HC than hot-start; ratios 1.1-1.5 (CO), 1.2-2.8 (HC); smaller engines (50 cm3) had higher ratios.
findings.value: 7 four-stroke carburetted + 2 fuel-injected motorcycles
findings.citation: Yao Y.-C., Tsai J.-H., Ye H.-F., Chiang H.-L. (2009) Comparison of exhaust emissions resulting from cold- and hot-start motorcycle driving modes. J. Air & Waste Manag. Assoc. 59(11):1339-1346
findings.quote: As expected, the emission factors (g/km) of CO and HCs increased during cold-start driving.
findings.caveats: Nine bikes; nothing about warm-engine stop-line idling.
findings.verifierNote: Verified in abstract.
findings.useOnSite: Cold engines emit more CO and hydrocarbons in Taiwanese tests.

findings.claim: Per-vehicle-km emission-factor estimates for Taiwan 2013-2021 rank motorcycles above gasoline vehicles for HC and above gasoline and diesel for benzene; formaldehyde ranked diesel > motorcycle >= gasoline.
findings.value: Benzene: motorcycle > gasoline >= diesel; HC: motorcycle > gasoline; four-stroke motorcycles 32.6% of road vehicle-km (abstract does not say which year; activity ~148-159 billion km/yr)
findings.citation: Tsai J.-H., Chen J.-Y., Chiang H.-L. (2023) Airborne air pollutant emission characteristics of mobile vehicles in Taiwan. Atmosphere 14(6):916
findings.quote: the emission sequence for benzene was motorcycle > gasoline ≥ diesel
findings.caveats: Modelled/compiled emission factors, not ambient concentration or share. Academic study (NCKU), not an official inventory. Abstract only.
findings.verifierNote: Quote verified in abstract. Corrected: '2021' attached to the 32.6% share is not stated in the abstract; 'official-style' wording removed. Motorcycles rank behind diesel and gasoline for PM2.5 and NOx.
findings.useOnSite: Modelled per-kilometre estimates put motorcycles above cars for benzene and hydrocarbon emission factors, but not for PM2.5 or NOx.

findings.claim: PAHs from one four-stroke motorcycle's diluted exhaust were mostly in fine particles with low-molecular-weight PAHs predominating; BaP-equivalent emission factor 70.8 +/- 38.4 ng/km.
findings.value: 77.0% of particulate PAH under 1.0 um, 84.3% under 2.5 um; mass median diameter 0.45 +/- 0.11 um; 21 PAHs, 0.056-18 um
findings.citation: Yang H.-H., Chien S.-M., Chao M.-R., Wang Y.-F. (2005) Size distribution of particulate polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons in the diluted four-stroke motorcycle exhausts. Aerosol Air Qual. Res. 5(2):225-235
findings.quote: Lower molecular weight PAHs predominate in motorcycle exhaust.
findings.caveats: One motorcycle. Only particulate-phase PAHs measured; gas-phase PAHs (e.g. naphthalene, which WHO says has a mothball odour with threshold 0.0075-0.42 mg/m3) were not. Do not say PAHs are odourless.
findings.verifierNote: Numbers verified in abstract. Removed the judgement 'low in absolute terms' (not in source) and the blanket 'mostly odourless' claim.
findings.useOnSite: One Taiwanese test measured particle-bound PAHs from a four-stroke motorcycle at 70.8 ng/km BaP-equivalent, mostly on sub-micron particles.

findings.claim: Nagata triangle-odor-bag detection thresholds (ppm): acetaldehyde 0.0015; acrolein 0.0036; styrene 0.035; m-xylene 0.041; p-xylene 0.058; ethylbenzene 0.17; 1,3-butadiene 0.23; toluene 0.33; 1-butene 0.36; o-xylene 0.38; formaldehyde 0.50; isopentane 1.3; n-pentane 1.4; 2-methylpentane 7.0; 3-methylpentane 8.9; benzene 2.7; propylene 13.
findings.value: as listed; 223 substances, experiments 1976-1988; lowest isoamyl mercaptan 0.77 ppt, highest propane 1500 ppm; CO not listed
findings.citation: Nagata Y. (Japan Environmental Sanitation Center) Measurement of odor threshold by triangle odor bag method (reproduced by the Japanese Ministry of the Environment)
findings.quote: Isoamyl mercaptane exhibited the lowest threshold (0.77ppt), and propane exhibited the highest threshold (1500ppm).
findings.caveats: Single compounds in clean air; panel-dependent. Publication year not shown in the PDF text I read; do not give a date such as 2003 without checking. 2-methylpentane and 3-methylpentane (main exhaust alkanes) smell only at 7-9 ppm, so they are not the smell.
findings.verifierNote: I downloaded and read the table; every value matches. Added 2-/3-methylpentane values, which weaken the case that the dominant alkanes drive the smell.
findings.useOnSite: Acetaldehyde and acrolein can be smelled at parts per billion; benzene only at parts per million.

findings.claim: EPA Hazard Summaries: benzene odour threshold 1.5 ppm (ATSDR-reported; AIHA detection 61 ppm, recognition 97 ppm); formaldehyde 0.83 ppm; acetaldehyde 0.05 ppm.
findings.value: as stated
findings.citation: US EPA Air Toxics Hazard Summaries: benzene, formaldehyde, acetaldehyde
findings.quote: Benzene has a sweet odor with an ASTDR reported odor threshold of 1.5 ppm (5 mg/m3).
findings.caveats: Old summaries; formaldehyde and acetaldehyde values trace to Amoore & Hautala 1983. Values differ from Nagata by 1-2 orders of magnitude.
findings.verifierNote: Opened all three PDFs; numbers match. Update dates not independently checked.
findings.useOnSite: Report odour thresholds as ranges with sources.

findings.claim: WHO reviewed formaldehyde odour thresholds (0.05-0.5 mg/m3; most studies 0.2-0.4) and concluded a significant fraction of the population may perceive it at or below 0.1 mg/m3, the level of its 30-minute guideline; perceiving it is not considered an adverse health effect.
findings.value: 0.05-0.5 mg/m3; guideline 0.1 mg/m3; naphthalene odour threshold 0.0075-0.42 mg/m3
findings.citation: WHO Regional Office for Europe (2010) WHO guidelines for indoor air quality: selected pollutants. Copenhagen: WHO
findings.quote: individuals may perceive formaldehyde at concentrations below 0.1 mg/m3. However, this is not considered to be an adverse health effect.
findings.caveats: Indoor-air document. WHO also notes eye and airway symptoms may be over-reported when odour cues are present.
findings.verifierNote: Read PDF text; all matched. Useful extra: WHO says odour cues can inflate reported irritation.
findings.useOnSite: Smelling formaldehyde is not itself proof of harm.

findings.claim: WHO (2010 indoor guidelines): CO is colourless, non-irritant, odourless and tasteless; benzene is a genotoxic carcinogen with no safe level of exposure; unit risk 6 x 10^-6 per ug/m3; 17, 1.7, 0.17 ug/m3 correspond to 1/10,000, 1/100,000, 1/1,000,000 excess lifetime leukaemia risk. CO guideline values listed there: 100 mg/m3 15 min, 35 mg/m3 1 h, 10 mg/m3 8 h, 7 mg/m3 24 h.
findings.value: as stated
findings.citation: WHO Regional Office for Europe (2010) WHO guidelines for indoor air quality: selected pollutants. Copenhagen: WHO
findings.quote: Benzene is a genotoxic carcinogen in humans and no safe level of exposure can be recommended.
findings.caveats: The 24-hour CO value (7 mg/m3) is from this 2010 document; my recollection is that the 2021 WHO global ambient air quality guidelines replaced it with 4 mg/m3 for 24 h, but I could not open that document (search budget exhausted), so verify before quoting a 24-hour CO figure. WHO text says indoor and ambient benzene guidance need not differ.
findings.verifierNote: All quoted text found in the PDF. Corrected by flagging the 24-hour CO value as possibly superseded.
findings.useOnSite: Carbon monoxide has no smell; WHO sets no safe level for benzene.

findings.claim: IARC Monographs Vol. 100F (2012) classifies benzene, 1,3-butadiene, formaldehyde and benzo[a]pyrene as Group 1.
findings.value: Group 1
findings.citation: IARC (2012) Chemical agents and related occupations. IARC Monogr. Eval. Carcinog. Risks Hum. 100F. Lyon: IARC
findings.quote: Volume 100 ... covers all agents previously classified by IARC as "carcinogenic to humans (Group 1)"
findings.caveats: Hazard, not risk at street doses. Mostly occupational evidence.
findings.verifierNote: I read the IARC volume page (title, year 2012, scope Group 1 agents only) but did not open the individual monograph PDFs, so the four per-agent statements rest on my knowledge plus the volume scope. Confidence downgraded to SECONDARY.
findings.useOnSite: State as a hazard classification only.

findings.claim: IARC Vol. 105 concluded gasoline exhaust is possibly carcinogenic (Group 2B), unchanged from 1989, while diesel exhaust is Group 1 (lung cancer; limited evidence for bladder).
findings.value: Gasoline 2B; diesel 1
findings.citation: IARC (2013) Diesel and gasoline engine exhausts and some nitroarenes. IARC Monogr. Eval. Carcinog. Risks Hum. 105. Lyon: IARC (evaluation meeting June 2012)
findings.quote: The Working Group concluded that gasoline exhaust was possibly carcinogenic to humans (Group 2B), a finding unchanged from the previous evaluation in 1989.
findings.caveats: Gasoline-exhaust evidence is mostly from cars, not scooters. Not 'scooter exhaust causes cancer'.
findings.verifierNote: Quote read on the IARC page, which lists the volume as IARC 2013. Other catalogues (PubMed, Crossref) may give 2014; check before print. The 'meeting 2012' detail is from memory, not the page.
findings.useOnSite: Gasoline exhaust is only 'possibly' carcinogenic (2B).

findings.claim: EPA Hazard Summaries: acute benzene inhalation may cause drowsiness, dizziness, headaches and eye, skin and respiratory irritation; formaldehyde causes eye, nose and throat irritation; acetaldehyde irritates eyes, skin and respiratory tract.
findings.value: qualitative
findings.citation: US EPA Air Toxics Hazard Summaries
findings.quote: Acute (short-term) inhalation exposure of humans to benzene may cause drowsiness, dizziness, headaches, as well as eye, skin, and respiratory tract irritation
findings.caveats: Effects at high, largely occupational exposures; no nausea statement found; old EPA cancer classifications in those documents are superseded.
findings.verifierNote: Text found in all three PDFs.
findings.useOnSite: Irritation and headache are known at high exposure; the question is dose.

findings.claim: Kuo et al. (2000) sampled VOCs for commuters on six Taichung roads; motorcycle commuters were generally exposed to higher VOC than car commuters. The specific numbers (2149/1343 ug/m3 on Ta-Ya Road, T:B:X:E 5.7:2.0:2.6:1.0) could not be re-checked.
findings.value: unverified numbers
findings.citation: Kuo H.-W., Wei H.-C., Liu C.-S., Lo Y.-Y., Wang W.-C., Lai J.-S., Chan C.-C. (2000) Exposure to volatile organic compounds while commuting in Taichung, Taiwan. Atmos. Environ. 34(20):3331-3336
findings.caveats: Late 1990s data; in-vehicle/rider exposure, not pedestrians.
findings.verifierNote: Crossref confirms title, authors, journal, volume, pages. The abstract could not be retrieved (OpenAlex and Crossref hold none; the NTU repository host is blocked), so I could not see the numbers or the quoted sentence. Do not publish the figures until the abstract is read.
findings.useOnSite: Do not use the numbers yet.

findings.claim: Kaohsiung ambient formaldehyde and acetaldehyde were the most abundant carbonyls at tens of ug/m3; gasoline vehicle exhaust was one of several sources in receptor modelling.
findings.value: Formaldehyde 17.99, acetaldehyde 13.69 ug/m3 (Nan-Chie); 21.47, 16.68 (Hsiung-Kong); together 56-57% of 18 carbonyls; summer total 74.06 / 89.99, winter 37.14 / 46.50 ug/m3
findings.citation: Wang H.-K., Huang C.-H., Chen K.-S., Peng Y.-P. (2010) Seasonal variation and source apportionment of atmospheric carbonyl compounds in urban Kaohsiung, Taiwan. Aerosol Air Qual. Res. 10(6):559-570
findings.quote: Formaldehyde and acetaldehyde were the most abundant carbonyls with respective annual mean concentrations of 17.99 μg/m3 and 13.69 μg/m3 at Nan-Chie
findings.caveats: Urban sites, 2006, not kerbside; scooters not separated from cars; secondary formation and restaurants contribute. Note the annual-mean figures sit above Nagata's acetaldehyde odour threshold only if converted (13.69 ug/m3 is about 7.6 ppb vs 1.5 ppb threshold), but this is general urban air, not a plume.
findings.verifierNote: Verified in abstract.
findings.useOnSite: Ordinary Taiwanese urban air already carries formaldehyde and acetaldehyde from many sources.

findings.claim: Five southern Taiwan tunnels showed toluene means from 1.6 to 115.8 ug/m3; Guogang Tunnel had the highest average MTBE and BTEX overall, Zhongliao the highest toluene mean (115.8; range 43.7-197.1).
findings.value: toluene means: Liangshan 1.6, Yueguangshan 17.6, Zoying 13.1, Guogang 57.5, Zhongliao 115.8 ug/m3
findings.citation: Hsieh L.-T., Wang Y.-F., Yang H.-H., Mi H.-H. (2011) Measurements and correlations of MTBE and BTEX in traffic tunnels. Aerosol Air Qual. Res. 11(6):763-775
findings.quote: Results showed that Guogang Tunnel was the most polluted with the highest average levels of both MTBE and BTEX
findings.caveats: Enclosed tunnels; fleet mix not scooter-specific; abstract has a typo in the first tunnel's range (5.6-6.2 with mean 1.6).
findings.verifierNote: Numbers verified. Original implied Zhongliao was the most polluted; the abstract says Guogang had the highest average BTEX overall.
findings.useOnSite: Tunnel data show buildup in enclosed traffic, not an open crossing.

findings.claim: Downtown Kaohsiung VOCs generally decreased with height (2-111 m), peaked in the 7-9 a.m. rush hour, and BTEX at all heights was mostly associated with ground-level vehicle activity.
findings.value: no concentrations in abstract
findings.citation: Lin C.-C., Lin C., Hsieh L.-T., Chen C.-Y., Wang J.-P. (2011) Vertical and diurnal characterization of volatile organic compounds in ambient air in urban areas. J. Air & Waste Manag. Assoc. 61(7):714-720
findings.quote: BTEX at all heights were mostly associated with vehicle transportation activities on the ground.
findings.caveats: Vehicles not split into scooters and cars; no numbers.
findings.verifierNote: Corrected: the abstract notes exceptions (higher at 13 m than ground at night, 32 m above 13 m at 7-9 a.m.), so 'ground-level highest' is too strong.
findings.useOnSite: Traffic at ground level was the main BTEX source in a Kaohsiung downtown study.

findings.claim: Taiwanese Phase III motorcycle exhaust OFP was dominated by propylene, isopentane, methylpentanes and toluene and was higher for in-use than new bikes.
findings.value: mg-O3/km (2-/4-stroke): propylene 65/502; isopentane 98/501; 2-methylpentane 152/167; 3-methylpentane 79/253; toluene 127/398; formaldehyde 4.1 (new)/6.2 (in-use); acetaldehyde 4.8/9
findings.citation: Tsai J.-H. et al. (2003) J. Air & Waste Manag. Assoc. 53(5):516-522
findings.quote: The ozone formation potentials, based on an ECE test cycle, show that the values from the in-use motorcycles were higher than those from the new motorcycles.
findings.caveats: Theoretical reactivity weights, not measured ozone; Phase III only.
findings.verifierNote: All numbers verified in the PubMed abstract.
findings.useOnSite: Scooter exhaust contains reactive hydrocarbons that can feed ozone formation.

findings.claim: Nguyen, Hsieh, Liang, Lin, Wang, Wang (2026) used hourly PAMS data from three Kaoping-region stations with PMF (eight NMHC sources); petroleum-related emissions dominate NMHC mass, while mixed vehicular and solvent sources contribute less mass but dominate OFP because of reactivity.
findings.value: eight sources; three PAMS stations
findings.citation: Nguyen et al. (2026) Multi-site non-methane hydrocarbon source apportionment and ozone insights in Southern Taiwan using positive matrix factorization. Atmos. Chem. Phys. 26:2831-2852 (published 2026-02-26)
findings.quote: Although mixed sources from vehicular and solvent emissions contributed less mass, they dominated ozone formation potential (OFP) due to higher chemical reactivity.
findings.caveats: The source is a mixed vehicular-solvent factor; motorcycles are not isolated. Given-name initials not retrieved.
findings.verifierNote: Upgraded from SECONDARY: I found the DOI via Crossref and read the abstract via OpenAlex. Authors and issue now identified.
findings.useOnSite: In southern Taiwan, a mixed traffic-and-solvent source made up little NMHC mass but dominated ozone-forming potential.

findings.claim: A Taipei Times item dated 2 August 2026 reportedly cites a poll (87.9% complained of exhaust fumes, 59% wore masks, 95% thought exhaust harms health).
findings.citation: Taipei Times (2026-08-02) article 2003861804
findings.caveats: Unknown sponsor, sample, scooter vs car.
findings.verifierNote: Direct fetch returned HTTP 403 again; I could not confirm the figures or the article exists as described.
findings.useOnSite: Do not use.

findings.claim: Comparator from another Asian city: jeepney drivers in Manila had average personal benzene exposure of 55.6 ug/m3 versus urban ambient 11.8 ug/m3.
findings.citation: Abstract of Manila jeepney driver VOC study, Ind Health 47:33 (DOI 10.2486/indhealth.47.33); authors and exact citation not checked
findings.quote: Personal sampling was conducted on 15 jeepney drivers.
findings.caveats: Diesel jeepneys, not scooters; occupational drivers; the Philippines. Retrieved incidentally by a title search; relevance to scooters is weak.
findings.verifierNote: Abstract read through Europe PMC/OpenAlex; citation metadata not checked in Crossref. Include only as a label-as-non-scooter comparator, or leave out.
findings.useOnSite: Not recommended for the site.

doNotClaim: Do not say the smell of exhaust measures how harmful the air is: CO and ultrafine particles are odourless.

Do not say benzene is what you smell: its threshold (about 1.5-97 ppm by source) is far above typical street levels; likely smellable contributors are aldehydes, alkenes and alkylbenzenes, but no study identifies the dominant odorants of scooter exhaust.
Do not say the dominant exhaust alkanes (2-/3-methylpentane, thresholds about 7-9 ppm) are the smell.
Do not present IARC Group 1 as a cancer risk at a crosswalk; gasoline exhaust as a mixture is only 2B, and no IARC classification of 'scooter exhaust' exists.
Do not state that pedestrians at Taiwanese red lights breathe above-guideline benzene, formaldehyde or CO: no such measurement was found.
Do not quote odour thresholds as single numbers; sources differ by 1-2 orders of magnitude.

Do not claim idle emits more per second or that idle drives the smell from this evidence: no idle-only figures were retrieved and the Taichung study attributes emissions mainly to technology and maintenance.
Do not call two-stroke exhaust a major part of today's fleet.
Do not cite the Taipei Times poll or the Kuo 2000 numbers until read.
Do not claim exhaust odour causes nausea or headache in pedestrians as established; WHO also notes odour cues can inflate reported irritation.
Do not describe PAHs as odourless in general: only particle-bound PAHs were measured.
Do not quote a 24-hour WHO CO value of 7 mg/m3 without checking the 2021 guidelines.
gaps: Idle-only speciated scooter emissions (Tsai 2003 full text).
Two-stroke lubricating-oil smoke: no quantitative Taiwanese source.
Taiwanese scooter acrolein and 1,3-butadiene emission factors.
IARC acetaldehyde classification (believed 2B, Vol. 71, 1999) and Vol. 46 (1989) not opened; per-agent text of Vol. 100F not opened.
ATSDR/IRIS not reachable; acute effects from older EPA Hazard Summaries.
Kerbside Taiwanese benzene/CO/formaldehyde versus background and scooter-specific source apportionment: not found.
Taiwanese resident survey on exhaust smell; the Taipei Times poll still unverified.
Evidence that exhaust odour causes nausea or headache.
Current MOENV inspection idle CO/HC limits.
WHO 2021 global AQG CO values not read.
Ultrafine particle emissions and health (outside scope).
Web search budget was exhausted during this check, which limited gap-closing.
